lesson.title: The Builder Enzyme: How DNA Polymerase Assembles a New Strand
lesson.summary: DNA polymerase is the enzyme that physically builds new DNA strands during replication, and its strict operating rules, always building 5' to 3' and always needing a primer to start, shape almost everything about how replication actually works.
lesson.body:
DNA replication is carried out by a team of proteins, but the central player is DNA polymerase, an enzyme in the truest sense of the word: a protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction without being consumed by it. Just as other enzymes lower the energy barrier for reactions like breaking down sugars, DNA polymerase lowers the energy barrier for linking nucleotides together, catalyzing the formation of the chemical bond (a phosphodiester bond) that connects one nucleotide to the next in a growing DNA strand.

DNA polymerase follows two rules that turn out to have huge consequences for how replication is organized. First, it can only add new nucleotides to the 3' end of an existing strand, which means it always builds DNA in the 5' to 3' direction, and it always reads the template strand in the opposite direction, 3' to 5'. Second, DNA polymerase cannot start a brand new strand from nothing. It can only extend an existing strand that already has a free 3'-OH group to attach the next nucleotide to. That starting piece is called a primer, a short stretch of nucleotides (usually RNA, laid down by a separate enzyme called primase) that gives DNA polymerase a foothold to begin working from.

To see the enzyme in action, imagine a short template strand reading 3'-GATTACA-5'. Reading that template in the 3' to 5' direction, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides one at a time to the 3' end of the new strand, matching each template base to its complementary partner: G pairs with C, A pairs with T, T pairs with A, and so on, producing a new strand that reads 5'-CTAATGT-3'. Notice that the new strand is antiparallel to its template, running in the opposite direction, which is a direct result of DNA polymerase's one-way, 5' to 3' building rule.

Cells actually use more than one kind of DNA polymerase, with different versions specialized for different jobs, such as bulk strand synthesis versus filling in small gaps left behind during replication. But the core behavior, extend an existing 3' end, read the template 3' to 5', build the new strand 5' to 3', is shared by all of them. As the next few chapters show, this single set of rules explains why replication proceeds the way it does at the molecular level, from the semiconservative arrangement of old and new strands to the very different way the two strands of the double helix are copied at a replication fork.
